note: Look, not law. Absorb or drop next sitting. A spark is not a trap.

items.claim: The qwen-code seat recipe passes the packet as an argv string, and on Windows a 33 KB packet exceeds the command-line limit: the seat dies with 'Argument list too long' before it reads a byte.
items.whyNotLaw: Observed once on F33's launch. The fix is stdin rather than argv, but no check yet proves a recipe can carry a packet of cap size on the platform the control plane sits on.

items.claim: An issuance commit pushed to main without a skip-ci marker turns the gate red and launches the GHA writer on the lane just issued, onto the same branch a local worktree already holds.
items.whyNotLaw: On F33 the cloud seat started headless with yolo on writer/F33 and was stopped only by a 401 on a stale DashScope secret. The F31 sitting knew this and wrote it as a ledger sentence, not a check.

items.claim: A router exists and one caller ignores it: ghaWriter.mjs hardcodes the DashScope base URL and maps the model through its own HOSTED table, so the cloud seat cannot take the native path route.mjs resolves for the local seat.
items.whyNotLaw: It also counts DEEPSEEK_API_KEY as having a writer secret but never passes it to the call, so a repo holding only that secret stops idling and then fails on an empty key, which is the loud skip T55 requires turned into a loud failure.

items.claim: A writer key read from a process environment is a value carried from an earlier act, not read from the store that owns it: after a rotation the User scope answers 200 and every already-open shell keeps answering 401.
items.whyNotLaw: Cost this sitting two wrong diagnoses and nearly a handover command that could not work. T04 names the shape and no recipe reads the key from its store in the same act as the launch.

items.claim: The seat census matches any command line containing qwen, aider, goose or opencode as a word, so an unrelated process reads as a running writer seat.
items.whyNotLaw: Caught live during F37's review: the reviewer's own 'pip show aider-chat' was reported as two running aider seats. A census that over-reports is a census that gets ignored, and no check distinguishes a harness process from a mention of one.

items.claim: A seat cited evidence that does not exist: a lane log named a git ref as the source of a price claim, and the ref appears nowhere in the repository except the sentence claiming it.
items.whyNotLaw: The underlying claim was true and derivable from route.mjs, so a reviewer reading for plausibility passes it. T02 covers a copied number and T56 a missing command; neither covers an invented reference, and nothing checks that a ref or path a log cites resolves.

items.claim: Half a fix can ship untested when one mutation reds for the other half's reason: splitCheck is case-sensitive AND last-wins, and only case-sensitivity has a fixture.
items.whyNotLaw: Restoring first-match while keeping case-sensitivity leaves alumni --self-test green, because no fixture row carries two capital-C directives. The envelope named one mutation combining both halves, and it reds on the first half alone.

items.claim: seat.mjs disjoint is pairwise and silently drops every argument past the second: 'disjoint F40 F41 F42' prints a verdict about F40/F41 and exits 0, so a control plane proving three siblings gets a green that covers one pair of the three.
items.whyNotLaw: Caught on the first act of sitting 11, by a control plane running the command the board's Now line cites for a mutual-disjointness claim about three lanes. The claim is true here - all three pairs were run by hand and each printed none shared - but the named command cannot mean what the sentence says. No check drives an extra argument, and the tool's own doc comment says 'disjoint <LANE> <LANE>' while the CLI accepts more without complaint.

items.claim: The gated 'seat packet' band measures seatPacket(root, null), the packet with no lane and so without the envelope: with F40 issued sizeBudget prints 99.7 per cent of 26 KB while packet.mjs seat F40 prints 31.6 KB.
items.whyNotLaw: Two readings, and the control plane could not settle it from the objects. Either the band measures a different object than the one that reaches a writer, which is D-59's family in the gate's own hand, or it is deliberately the byte-stable cacheable prefix at 26 with the envelope budgeted separately at 6, total about 32, in which case one label for two numbers 5.7 KB apart is what needs fixing. budgets.json's note and D-57 both speak of 'the packet' at 25.3 KB, which is the prefix reading. Settle it before the next ceiling argument: a control plane reading 99.7 per cent green can hand a seat 22 per cent more context than the number it just checked.

items.claim: The census counts processes, not seats: two qwen-code launches produced six rows, a cli-entry wrapper plus --expose-gc children each, and it printed 6 running writer seat(s) when the true number was two.
items.whyNotLaw: Observed live when sitting 11's two siblings were launched, with the real number known. F40 does NOT fix this: that lane puts the harness token in program position, and every one of the six rows has it there, so the count stays wrong by the process tree after F40 lands. The two-writer ceiling and the dead-seat resume both read this number. A seat is a process group, or the row a launch recorded, not a matching command line.

items.claim: A correction envelope is written to main, but a seat reads its envelope from its own worktree, which still holds the superseded page; git fetch does not touch the working tree, so the seat runs the old envelope silently.
items.whyNotLaw: Caught live this sitting by reading the envelope's first line after launching: the F42 correction seat was started against the original envelope, stopped, and relaunched only after the worktree was rebased onto main. packet.mjs reads factory/envelopes/<LANE>.md from the tree it runs in, so the failure is invisible and looks like a seat ignoring its instructions. Nothing in seat.mjs, the recipe or the packet warns that a correction launch must rebase the worktree first, and the cost is a whole paid session spent against a stale page.
